source_review.notes: Retrieved and reviewed the primary System R, Cascades, optimizer-evaluation, statistical resource-estimation, robust plan-evaluation, and learned-cost-model papers; PostgreSQL 18 planner, EXPLAIN, and index-cost documentation plus current costsize.c commentary; current Calcite cost interface; and current Redshift plan/distribution documentation. Checked units, startup/total and cumulative semantics, partial consumption, physical properties, cost components, distributed movement, calibration cautions, learned-model scope, and uncertainty claims.

evidence: Checked P, x, O, resource vectors, startup/total cost, scalar score, weights, feasible set, critical path, crossover, residual, and regret definitions.
Checked processed/emitted rows, logical/physical I/O, aggregate/elapsed CPU, network bytes/time, and allocation/peak memory remain distinct.
Checked every displayed equation names compatible dimensions and its modeling assumptions.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Arbitrary score units are consistently distinguished from milliseconds and physical resource units.

evidence: Independently recomputed scan total 2250.00, selective index 367.75, broad index 5352.00, and both access-path choices.
Recomputed first-row interpolation 5.6575 versus 201, nested-loop repeated work 300 versus 30000, and spill underestimate factor 1.555556.
Recomputed broadcast/repartition bytes, parallel critical/busy time, and risk-aware scores in artifacts/reviews/DBE-065/independent-recomputation.txt.
numerical_recomputation.notes: Independent Decimal arithmetic and assertions passed without importing the chapter executable.

evidence: Reviewed positive common-scaling equivalence in both directions for k greater than zero.
Reviewed constrained argmin formulation and why feasibility precedes scalar comparison.
Reviewed scan/index crossover, conditional optimal substructure, startup/total interpolation, and parallel critical-path composition.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The partial-consumption and critical-path equations are explicitly scoped as models with declared preconditions, not universal identities.

evidence: Reviewed empty and zero-row plans, LIMIT/early stop, blocking startup, cumulative-cost double counting, repeated/shared work, and impossible physical-property transfers.
Reviewed cache extremes, index clustering, variable widths, memory threshold/spill, worker unavailability, skew, bandwidth contention, broadcast duplication, and temp exhaustion.
Reviewed timeout censoring, optimizer-selected training bias, OOD operators/hardware/workloads, noisy feedback, tenant privacy/poisoning, model inference failure, canary containment, and rollback.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Hard constraints and unsupported states are not disguised as large finite soft costs.

evidence: Checked each cost is bound to plan, properties, estimates, parameters, environment, resource/concurrency class, generation, objective, and units.
Checked child execution events are charged once and serial, parallel, repeated, shared, cached, blocking, and pipelined lifetimes remain distinguishable.
Checked calibration, learned-model, shadow, canary, and rollback records retain coverage, versions, limitations, and safe fallback.
invariant_checking.notes: Correctness and feasibility are gates before optimization, and selected-plan outcomes remain separate from prediction accuracy.

evidence: Reviewed the positive-scaling proof using order preservation and division by a positive scalar.
Reviewed conditional optimal-substructure reasoning over logical group plus physical properties and resource state.
Reviewed critical-path proof sketch and the separation from aggregate resource work.
proof_review.notes: No universal optimality theorem, latency equivalence, or calibrated uncertainty guarantee is claimed.

evidence: The critical-path argument is labeled a proof sketch with overlap and resource assumptions.
The executable is labeled deterministic normalized arithmetic rather than a database benchmark.
System R, Cascades, PostgreSQL, Redshift, statistical, learned, and robust-model results are scoped to their papers, products, interfaces, and studied settings.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Analytical equations, implementation documentation, empirical findings, and production policy are kept distinct.

evidence: Repository verification passed one standard-library Python snippet with exact thirteen-line stdout, empty stderr, zero exit status, and recorded Python 3.14.4 toolchain.
Independent recomputation passed sixteen printed checks covering access paths, partial consumption, repeated work, spill, movement, parallelism, robustness, and scaling.
All thirteen source artifacts were retained under artifacts/references/DBE-065 and local Markdown links were checked.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No live DBMS plan, hardware calibration, distributed cluster, learned model, workload replay, canary, security test, or external review was run.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed the decision-model boundary, cost vectors/scalars, properties and enforcers, startup/total work, operator formulas, composition, calibration, evaluation, learned/hybrid models, uncertainty, and production control.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed first-divergence diagnosis, resource and concurrency context, spill/broadcast/parallel hazards, explain-trace semantics, representative calibration, OOD/fallback, shadowing, controlled canaries, observability, kill switches, privacy, and rollback.

pedagogical_review.notes: The chapter derives cost decisions from first principles, executes a multi-decision finite model, covers fourteen misconceptions and ten distinct examples, and progresses through five exercises to a complete hybrid-model evidence and rollout design.

limitations: Internal authoring, primary/official-source, mathematical, executable-snippet, conceptual, practitioner, and pedagogical evidence only; no external database researcher, optimizer maintainer, performance engineer, distributed-systems operator, ML reviewer, security/privacy reviewer, platform owner, or educator review is claimed. The chapter and finite arithmetic prove neither accurate costs on any live DBMS, representative hardware calibration, optimal plan selection, learned-model generalization, calibrated uncertainty, workload improvement, fairness, privacy, certification, nor deployment fitness.
